[ITQAN:v1p234/r9] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | Kallā occurs thirty-three times; seven are unanimously rebukes at which pausing is permitted, including the examples listed. | mentions 19:82, 26:15
[BURSEVI:v5p272#3/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The interrogative has two hamzas; the root means climbing to a mountain's top or a mountain pass.
[BURSEVI:v5p272#3/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The taunt asks whether he reached God's unique knowledge of the unseen or made a covenant with its Knower; only those routes could disclose future wealth and children.
[BURSEVI:v5p272#3/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | reports | Another view takes the covenant as testimony of faith and righteous action, for which God promised reward.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p130#2/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The question أطلع الغيب rebuts the outrageous claim and is a fresh sentence; treating it as the second object of “tell me” is judged unlikely.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p130#2/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | A reading with kasra on the initial hamza omits the interrogative hamza, whose presence is indicated by أم, as in the cited poetic question.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p130#2/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | طلع is directly transitive, though it can take على; the image is ascent into possession of hidden knowledge, not ordinary knowing.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p130#2/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The question challenges whether al-ʿĀṣī has mastered God's exclusive unseen knowledge to assert his future wealth and children.

[ALUSI-FULL:v16p130#2/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · ابن عباس | reports | He interprets the covenant as professing that there is no deity but God and hoping for the promised reward.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p130#2/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · قتادة | reports | Qatada takes the covenant as righteous work for which God promised reward; another view understands a literal pledge from God that the claim will certainly occur.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p130#2/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الكلبي | reports | The literal-covenant view is a rhetorical concession to the sinner's own wording; calling God al-Rahman invokes mercy as the supposed ground of the promised grant.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v16p159/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The reply uses the wise rhetorical strategy of taking his words literally: did he inspect the unseen and verify the afterlife wealth he claims? The question denies and ridicules the claim.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v16p159/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Iṭṭalaʿa is a strengthened form of ṭalaʿa, originally intransitive; when it means “look over,” it takes ʿalā, as illustrated by 37:54–55 and 18:18. | mentions 37:54, 37:55, 18:18
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v16p159/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Al-ghayb is a direct object, not a preposition left unspoken as some commentators assume; al-Zamakhsharī says the word depicts an audacious ascent to knowledge of the unseen.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v16p159/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | His boast could mean he saw wealth and children waiting in the afterlife, or saw his existing family accompanying him there; either requires access to the unseen.

[TABATABAI:19:80/r4] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · الأكثر | reports | On the majority reading, the speaker is ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil or al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra, who swears he will receive wealth and children in Paradise after resurrection; God asks whether he knows the unseen or has a covenant, then strips him of possessions and brings him alone.
